title: Indigenous Music Traditions
subtitle: Two gong traditions, north and south, and how each is struck.
objectives: Name the main indigenous Philippine music traditions
Say where each tradition comes from
Explain why this music is tied to an occasion

cards.title: Not folk music. Living traditions, with addresses.
cards.text: "Ethnic music" flattens a hundred groups into one word. These traditions have regions, techniques and rules, and they are still played.

cards.title: Two great gong traditions, north and south
cards.text: The Philippines has two, and they are not the same.
points: **The Cordillera, north:** flat gongs called **gangsa**.
**Mindanao, south:** a row of tuned gongs, the **kulintang**.
**Flat and hand-struck** in the north.
**Bossed and melodic** in the south.

cards.title: Six indigenous traditions, and how each is played
cards.text: Tap each one. The second line is how it is actually played.

question.explain: Flat gongs, played in the northern highlands.

cards.title: Two ways to play a gangsa
cards.text: The method has a name, and it changes the whole sound.
points: **Toppaya:** seated, struck with the **palm**.
**Palook:** standing or walking, struck with a **stick**.
**Same instrument**, two different events.
**The technique tells you the occasion.**

cards.title: Nobody counts out loud
cards.text: In a gong ensemble each player holds one part and listens for the others.
points: **No conductor.** No sheet music.
**You learn it by standing in it.**
**Same as learning a combination:** by repetition, not description.
**Lose the timing** and the whole pattern collapses.

options: Playing with a stick while standing
question.explain: The other technique is toppaya: seated, with the palm.

cards.title: This music has a job
cards.text: It is not written for a concert hall, and that changes everything about it.
points: **Rituals:** healing, harvest, funerals.
**Courtship:** the kudyapi and the kubing are played close and quiet.
**Celebration:** weddings and victory, with the full ensemble.
**Taught by ear**, passed down by playing. Not by notation.

cards.title: Why a gong's size sets its note
cards.text: The same rule you met last week, in bronze.
points: **Bigger and thicker** vibrates slower. Lower note.
**Smaller and thinner** vibrates faster. Higher note.
**A kulintang row** is eight gongs graded by size.
**Nothing is adjusted while playing.** The tuning is in the metal.

cards.title: A kulintang row, graded by size
cards.alt: Eight graded bronze gongs on a carved wooden frame with two padded beaters, and a larger flat gong behind
cards.text: Eight gongs, smallest to largest. The tuning is in the metal, not in a knob.

cards.title: A tradition with no text
cards.text: When nothing is written down, the music itself is the archive.
points: **A forgotten piece is gone.** There is no copy.
**That is why recording these traditions matters.**
**The Darangen was chanted**, not read, for centuries.
**Every performer is a link** in a chain that can break.

cards.title: What to remember
points: Cordillera: flat gangsa gongs, played toppaya or palook.
Mindanao: the tuned kulintang row, with agung and gandingan beneath.
Kudyapi is a two-string lute; kubing a jaw harp.
The music belongs to an occasion, and is learned by ear.

teacher.summary: Term 2 Week 2 MAPEH, Music strand. The week's purpose is to replace the single word 'ethnic' with addresses and techniques: two distinct gong traditions, north and south, and the named methods of striking a gangsa. Toppaya and palook do real work here, because a technique with a name is a fact he can hold, while 'indigenous music' is not. The pitch rule from week 1 is carried over into bronze so the two weeks reinforce rather than sit apart. The last card makes the point that an oral tradition has no backup copy, which is why recording it matters.
discussion: Ask which tradition is north and which is south.
Ask what the difference is between toppaya and palook.
Ask why a kulintang row is graded by size.
Ask what is lost when an oral tradition stops being played.
extension: Find a kulintang recording and have him count the gongs he can hear.
Have him tap a pattern and keep it while you play a different one.
misconceptions: "All Philippine gongs are the same." Flat and hand-struck north; tuned and bossed south.
"This music is for performances." It belongs to occasions.
"It is written down somewhere." It is learned by ear.
